claims.claim: Therapeutic communication is the most used form of communication in health care: a specialized form of communication used by healthcare professionals to establish a therapeutic or healing relationship with patients.

The concept of therapeutic communication was developed in the 1950s to provide therapeutic benefit, and nursing theorist Hildegard Peplau's Theory of Interpersonal Relations established therapeutic communication as a way to advance the healing process in patients.
Therapeutic communication includes both verbal and nonverbal components and is used in all communication encounters with patients.
Therapeutic communication techniques include active listening, empathy, silence, asking relevant questions, and open-ended questions, which support therapeutic communication.
Reflection on the response — restating what the patient said — lets the patient hear their own words, encourages them to continue, and shows the nurse is actively listening.

Nontherapeutic communication — negative expressions, attitudes, and actions that make a patient feel uneasy — includes giving advice, false reassurance, and changing the subject, and can lead to miscommunication that affects the care the patient receives.
Nurses evaluate the effectiveness of therapeutic communication through a feedback loop: if the intended message was not received, the nurse revises the approach and tries again.

AHRQ's TeamSTEPPS is an evidence-based teamwork system aimed at optimizing patient outcomes by improving communication and teamwork skills among healthcare professionals, including patients and family caregivers, and its curriculum includes a Communication module.
The 2023 TeamSTEPPS update emphasizes active patient involvement in their care.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Different textbooks list different sets of therapeutic techniques (some add humor, touch, offering self, providing information).
positions: OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing lists providing information, sharing observations/feelings, empathy, hope, humor, touch, silence, clarifying, asking relevant questions, offering self, and active listening
This lesson names the five core techniques (active listening, open questions, reflecting, silence, empathy) per the topic scope
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that textbooks list a family of techniques and that five are worth mastering first; no claim of exhaustiveness is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Reflection vs. clarifying are sometimes treated as the same technique in different texts.
positions: OpenStax describes 'Reflect on the Response' as restating what the patient said
Some texts describe clarification as follow-up questioning to pin down meaning
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches reflection as restating the patient's words (the OpenStax description) and does not conflate it with clarifying.

positions: OpenStax describes silence as allowing the patient time to think and process, with the patient breaking the silence
Silence can also be avoidance when a caregiver withdraws from a hard topic
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson distinguishes deliberate therapeutic silence from avoidant silence in Compare / Contrast.
